options.label: D
options.text: Ruptured atherosclerotic plaque within coronary vessels

questions.solution: Correct Option A- Dilatation of coronary vessels: Dipyridamole is a phosphodiesterase type 3 inhibitor used for treating coronary stent restenosis and intermittent vascular claudication and as an antiplatelet (anti-angina, TIA/stroke prevention) drug. Dipyridamole induces coronary vasodilation by raising adenosine levels and activating adenosine A2A receptors. Myocardial ischemia brought on by a shift of blood flow is known as coronary steal syndrome. The seriously stenotic arteries' rigidity only permits a small coronary flow reserve. Blood is therefore directed to collaterals and healthy vessels when coronary arteries widen. As a result, there is tissue ischemia distal to the coronary artery stenosis , which causes chest tightness and novel ECG abnormalities. The adenosine or dipyridamole pharmacological stress test is based on this occurrence. Incorrect Options: Option B- Increased myocardial oxygen demand: The dobutamine stress test and the cardiac exercise stress test increase myocardial oxygen demand (MVO2). Dipyridamole influences myocardial oxygenation and coronary perfusion but has minimal effects on MVO2. Option C- Vasospasm of coronary arteries: The ECG changes observed in this patient's case would be caused by the vasospasm of coronary arteries , which is the source of Prinzmetal angina. However, unlike this patient, who complained of chest tightness with exertion, Prinzmetal angina patients usually experience symptoms at rest. Dipyridamole treatment, which causes vasodilation rather than vasospasm but also causes chest pain, indicates a different reason for this patient's symptoms. Option D- Ruptured atherosclerotic plaque within coronary vessels: The mechanism that causes acute coronary syndrome (ACS), which would result in chest tightness and the ECG changes observed here, is thrombotic occlusion of a coronary vessel after the rupture of a cholesterol plaque. Every stress test carries some risk for ACS, but the risk is minimal with a dipyridamole stress test because the drug prevents platelet coagulation. A different cause probably brought on chest tightness in this patient. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option B- Pregnancy termination should be discussed in patients who will become pregnant while they have the diagnosis: This statement is incorrect. Pregnancy termination is generally not recommended solely due to the diagnosis of essential thrombocytosis (ET). While there are increased risks associated with ET during pregnancy, including miscarriage and thrombosis, many women with ET successfully carry their pregnancies to term with appropriate monitoring and management. questions.solution: Correct Option B - Karyotype analysis: Klinefelter syndrome is a genetic disorder that affects males and is caused by the presence of an extra X chromosome. The diagnosis of Klinefelter syndrome is typically made through a combination of clinical evaluation and laboratory tests. Clinical Evaluation: The diagnosis of Klinefelter syndrome may be suspected based on physical examination findings, such as small testes, gynecomastia, reduced body hair, and tall stature. Other signs and symptoms that may suggest Klinefelter syndrome include delayed puberty, decreased muscle mass, and decreased libido. Laboratory Tests: Several laboratory tests can be used to support the diagnosis of Klinefelter syndrome. These include: Karyotype analysis: This is the gold standard for diagnosing Klinefelter syndrome. It involves analysing the patient's chromosomes to look for the presence of an extra X chromosome (47,XXY). This test can also detect other chromosomal abnormalities that may be associated with similar clinical features. Hormone levels: In Klinefelter syndrome, testosterone levels are typically low and levels of follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinising hormone (LH) are elevated. These hormone levels can be measured through blood tests. Semen analysis: Infertility is a common feature of Klinefelter syndrome, and semen analysis can be used to assess the patient's fertility status. Imaging studies: Ultrasound and MRI can be used to evaluate the size and structure of the testes and to look for other abnormalities that may be associated with Klinefelter syndrome. Neuropsychological testing: Klinefelter syndrome is associated with an increased risk of learning and behavioural difficulties, and neuropsychological testing can be used to assess these functions. Incorrect Options: Option A - Testosterone level: A low testosterone level is a common finding in Klinefelter syndrome, but it is not a definitive diagnostic test. It can be useful in assessing the severity of the disorder and monitoring treatment response. Option C - Prostate-specific antigen (PSA) level: PSA level is not typically used in the diagnosis of Klinefelter syndrome. It is a marker for prostate cancer and is not specific to this disorder. Blood work reveals a hemoglobin level of 9.5 g/dL and a serum creatinine level of 10 mg/dL. Which of the following strategies could improve her quality of life?
questions.solution: Correct Option C- Joining a support group: Dialysis can significantly impact the quality of life of patients with end-stage renal disease, and several strategies can be employed to improve the quality of life. One such strategy is joining a support group. Support groups can allow patients to connect with others going through similar experiences, share coping strategies, and receive emotional support. It can help patients feel less isolated and improve their overall well-being. Incorrect Options: Option A- Increasing dialysis frequency: It is incorrect because while increasing dialysis frequency may improve some symptoms, such as fluid overload, it may not necessarily improve quality of life. Additionally, more frequent dialysis may not be possible or practical for all patients. Option B- Starting a low-protein diet: It is incorrect because while diet modifications may be necessary for some patients with end-stage renal disease, a low-protein diet is not recommended for all dialysis patients. Many dialysis patients require a higher protein intake to help maintain muscle mass and prevent malnutrition. Option D- Decreasing the fluid intake: It is incorrect because while limiting fluid intake may be necessary for some patients with fluid overload, it can also lead to dehydration and other complications. Patients must work with their healthcare team to determine an appropriate fluid intake based on their needs. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 15-year-old African American boy presented to the clinic after an episode of gross hematuria. He has a history of excessive urination and wakes 2-3 times at night for urination. His physical examination shows no abnormalities. His mother died of a stroke when he was 2 years of age. Urinalysis show’s following: Specific gravity 1.005 Protein None Blood Moderate Red blood cells Many/hpf Which part of the kidney is affected in this patient?
questions.stemHtml:

His physical examination shows no abnormalities. His mother died of a stroke when he was 2 years of age. Urinalysis show’s following:
			Specific gravity
			1.005
			Protein
			None
			Blood
			Moderate
			Red blood cells
			Many/hpf
Which part of the kidney is affected in this patient?
questions.solution: Correct Option A: Renal papillae This patient presents with gross hematuria with complaints of polyuria with a low urine specific gravity consistent with hyposthenuria and the inability of the kidneys to concentrate urine, a feature of sickle cell disease. His family history is significant for early-onset stroke, which can be a severe complication of sickle cell disease (SCD) due to cerebrovascular occlusion from sickling. However, he has no other symptoms. Therefore, sickle cell trait (SCT) is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms. Sickle cell trait is a benign condition associated with hemoglobin AS that is more common in Africa, the Middle East, and Mediterranean countries and African American and Hispanic individuals. Hyposthenuria is common in patients with SCD and may also develop in those with SCT. In response to hypoxic, hyperosmolar conditions of the renal medulla, red blood cells sickle in the vasa recta, impairing free water reabsorption and countercurrent exchange. Patients typically have polyuria and nocturia despite fluid restriction. Urine osmolality is low; however, normal serum sodium is maintained due to intact antidiuretic hormone (ADH). Urinary diluting capacity is also intact as it is a function of the superficial loop of Henle, which is not supplied by the vasa recta. Non-glomerular hematuria is characterized by gross hematuria with normal-appearing red blood cells (RBCs) but without significant proteinuria. Etiologies include: Cancer (e.g. renal cell, prostate) Infections (e.g. cystitis) Polycystic kidney disease Nephrolithiasis Papillary necrosis Gross hematuria can be from: Bladder (e.g. cystitis. cancer) Renal (e.g. glomerulonephritis) Ureteral pathology (e.g. nephrolithiasis) Prostate pathology (e.g. benign prostatic hyperplasia) This patient's gross hematuria and urinalysis with normal-appearing red blood cells (RBCs) suggest an extra-glomerular etiology. Painless hematuria is likely due to renal papillary ischemia or necrosis. The relatively low local partial pressure of oxygen in the vasa recta predisposes the affected red blood cells to sickle. Papillary necrosis can occur with massive hematuria, but the episodes are usually mild and resolve spontaneously. The urinalysis usually shows normal-appearing RBCs. It may be associated with sickle cell disease/trait. Other renal complications include: Hyposthenuria; inability to concentrate the urine (vasa recta damage with an inability to maintain concentrated medullary gradient) Distal renal tubular acidosis (tubular damage with impaired H+ secretion). Incorrect options: Option B: Renal interstitium The renal interstitium refers to the connective tissue and extracellular matrix that comprise the space between the renal tubules and blood vessels in the kidney. The interstitium plays an important role in regulating renal function by providing support and structural organization for the various components of the kidney. One of the primary functions of the renal interstitium is to maintain the integrity of the renal tubules and blood vessels. The interstitium contains collagen fibers and other extracellular matrix components that support and help maintain the structural integrity of the kidney. The interstitium also contains various cells, including fibroblasts and macrophages, involved in tissue repair and immune defense. The interstitium is also important for regulating fluid and electrolyte balance in the kidney. The interstitial fluid communicates with the blood and the tubular fluid, exchanging ions and solutes between these compartments. The interstitium is also involved in the production and secretion of various hormones and growth factors that regulate renal function. Renal tumors or malignancies (e.g., renal cell cancer) involving the interstitium can present as non-glomerular hematuria. However, isosthenuria would not be typically seen with this condition. Option C: Glomerulus The glomerulus is a specialized structure in the kidney that plays a critical role in blood filtration and urine production. It is a small, spherical structure composed of a network of capillaries, known as glomerular capillaries, that is surrounded by a layer of specialized cells called podocytes. The glomerular capillaries are highly permeable, allowing water and small solutes to pass through the Bowman's capsule, the first part of the renal tubule. The podocytes, which have unique finger-like projections called foot processes, form a barrier that helps to regulate the passage of larger molecules, such as proteins, into the Bowman's capsule. Blood filtration in the glomerulus is regulated by complex interactions between the podocytes, mesangial cells, and the blood vessels that supply the glomerulus. These interactions help to maintain the proper balance of fluid and solutes in the body while preventing the loss of important molecules such as proteins. Glomerular hematuria refers to the presence of red blood cells in the urine that originate from the glomerulus in the kidney. This condition can be caused by several different physiological factors, which are as follows: Damage to the glomerular capillaries, e.g. glomerulonephritis, lupus nephritis, and vasculitis. Abnormalities in the structure or function of the glomerular filtration barrier, e.g. Alport syndrome. Abnormalities in platelet function or coagulation, e.g. thrombotic microangiopathy. Diseases of the glomerulus cause microscopic hematuria, though gross hematuria may be present in some cases. It is usually due to glomerulonephritis (GN or basement membrane disease. Symptoms are usually absent or nonspecific (e.g., low back pain), and patients may present after developing features of the nephritic syndrome (e.g., hematuria, hypertension, oliguria, elevated creatinine). Urinalysis usually shows proteinuria with dysmorphic RBCs or RBC casts. Option D: Renal Tubules Renal tubules are the microscopic tubes in the kidney that filter blood and produce urine. They are located in the nephrons, the kidney's functional units. The renal tubules comprise several distinct segments, each with a unique structure and function. Hematuria caused by the renal tubules, also known as tubular hematuria, refers to the presence of red blood cells in the urine originating from the kidney tubules. Causes of tubular hematuria include: Damage to the renal tubules, e.g. interstitial nephritis, polycystic kidney disease, and certain medications. Kidney stones. Bleeding disorders, such as von Willebrand disease or thrombocytopenia. Acute tubular necrosis is characterized by acute azotemia following a hypotensive or nephrotoxic injury. Patients may have dark or cola-coloured urine, but significant hematuria is uncommon. Tubulointerstitial nephritis causes microscopic hematuria associated with elevated creatinine and variable proteinuria. It is most commonly due to certain medications, including antibiotics, NSAIDs, and diuretics. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 54-year-old female patient undergoes radiation therapy as part of a treatment plan for endometrial cancer. Fourteen months after the completion of therapy, she presented with grade III small bowel radiation enteritis. Over the past 3 years, she has required multiple small bowel resections for management of her radiation enteritis. Which of the following strategies cannot be used to preserve small bowel length in this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 54-year-old female patient undergoes radiation therapy as part of a treatment plan for endometrial cancer. Fourteen months after the completion of therapy, she presented with grade III small bowel radiation enteritis. Over the past 3 years, she has required multiple small bowel resections for management of her radiation enteritis. Which of the following strategies cannot be used to preserve small bowel length in this patient?
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Total parenteral nutrition: The correct answer is C. Total parenteral nutrition (TPN): TPN is a method of delivering nutrition intravenously when a patient cannot consume food orally or through the gastrointestinal tract. While it provides essential nutrients, it does not address the underlying issue of small bowel length loss caused by radiation enteritis. TPN is a supportive measure used when other interventions, like surgical resection, are necessary due to severe complications. It does not prevent the need for small bowel resections in the management of radiation enteritis. Incorrect Options: Option A - Stricturoplasty: It is a surgical procedure used to widen strictures (narrowed segments) in the small intestine caused by conditions like Crohn's disease. It is not directly related to preserving small bowel length and is not applicable in the context of radiation enteritis, which is a different condition. Option B - Intestinal-lengthening procedure: This option refers to surgical procedures that aim to increase the length of the intestines, typically used in patients with short bowel syndrome. While this procedure may be considered in certain cases of short bowel syndrome, it is not a common strategy for preserving small bowel length in the context of radiation enteritis. Option D - Hyperbaric oxygen therapy: Hyperbaric oxygen therapy involves breathing pure oxygen in a pressurized room or chamber, and it is sometimes used as an adjunctive treatment for radiation enteritis. It helps improve oxygen delivery to the affected tissues and promotes wound healing, but it does not directly address preserving small bowel length. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 62 year old female patient presents to you with an 8 cm heterogeneous appearing contrast-enhancing mass of the right kidney, invading into the adrenal gland. There is no associated adenopathy or distant spread. What is the TNM score and stage?
questions.stemHtml: A 62 year old female patient presents to you with an 8 cm heterogeneous appearing contrast-enhancing mass of the right kidney, invading into the adrenal gland. There is no associated adenopathy or distant spread. What is the TNM score and stage?
questions.solution: Correct Option D - T4 N0 M0 -stage IV The tumor size is 8 cm, which corresponds to T4 in the TNM staging system. T4 indicates that the tumor has invaded nearby structures, such as the adrenal gland. There is no evidence of regional lymph node involvement (N0). There is no evidence of distant metastasis (M0). Therefore, the TNM score for this patient is T4 N0 M0, which corresponds to stage IV kidney cancer. Stage IV indicates that the cancer has extended beyond the kidney and invaded nearby structures, in this case, the adrenal gland. While there is no regional lymph node involvement or distant metastasis, the invasion into the adrenal gland classifies it as stage IV due to the advanced local spread. Incorrect Options: Option A - T2 N0 M0 - stage II T2 typically indicates a tumor size of 7 cm or smaller that is confined to the kidney. Since the patient's tumor is 8 cm and has invaded the adrenal gland, T2 is not the appropriate classification. The absence of lymph node involvement and distant metastasis (N0 M0) would typically be associated with earlier stages. Option B - T2 N0 M0 - stage III Again, T2 typically indicates a smaller tumor confined to the kidney. The patient's tumor is larger and has invaded the adrenal gland, making T2 inappropriate. questions.solution: Correct Option C - Order HCV RNA testing Screening for hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection is done by testing for the anti-HCV antibody. If the anti-HCV antibody is positive, then confirmation testing should be pursued by performing HCV RNA testing. Screening should be considered in adults born between 1945 and 1965, intravenous drug users, persons who received clotting factor concentrates produced before 1987, persons who were ever on long-term hemodialysis, persons with persistently abnormal alanine aminotransferase (ALT) levels, persons who have HIV infection, persons who received prior transfusions or organ transplants from an HCV-positive donor or if the transfusion or organ transplants occurred before July 1992, children born to HCV-positive women, and health care workers who experienced needle sticks from HCV-positive patients. Incorrect Options: Option A - Consult hepatology: Infection should be confirmed by HCV RNA testing before consulting hepatology for therapy. Option B - Order hepatic function tests: There is no need for hepatic function testing in confirming infection with HCV. Option D - Repeat serum HCV antibody: The initial anti-HCV antibody is positive and repeating it will not add information to guide management. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option D - Prophylactic thyroidectomy: This young female with a palpable mass in the neck is found to have a euthyroid goit re. However, her genetic testing is significant for RET proto-oncogene mutation , associated with an increased risk of medullary thyroid cancer . Therefore the best step in her management would be to perform a prophylactic thyroidectomy. Individuals with RET gene mutation have an increased risk of developing medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC) associated with MEN 2A, 2B . MTC is a parafollicular C-cell tumor in the thyroid gland, which produces calcitonin . Prophylactic thyroidectomy involves surgical removal of the thyroid gland. It is the most effective way to reduce the risk of developing medullary thyroid cancer in patients with a RET gene mutation. Incorrect Options: Option A - Observation with serial imaging studies: This monitors the patient's thyroid gland through imaging studies, such as ultrasound or CT scans, at regular intervals to track any changes in the size or appearance of the goitre. However, observation alone is not recommended given the patient's family history of thyroid carcinoma, and RET gene mutation indicates a high risk of medullary thyroid cancer. This approach may be appropriate for patients with a small, asymptomatic goitre that is not suspicious of cancer. Annual surveillance with serum calcitonin levels is recommended in patients with RET proto-oncogene mutation . Calcitonin is the serum marker specific for medullary thyroid cancer, not with serum thyroxine levels. Option C - Iodine supplementation: Iodine supplementation is used to treat iodine deficiency. However, in this case, the patient has a euthyroid goitre, meaning her thyroid hormone levels are within the normal range, and therefore iodine supplementation is not indicated . questions.solution: Correct Option D - Trial of migraine prophylaxis with ibuprofen abortive therapy: This patient has a Chiari I malformation on MRI, defined as 5 mm herniation of one or both cerebellar tonsils below the foramen magnum, with evidence of crowding of the subarachnoid spaces adjacent to the medulla and cerebellum. Headaches associated with Chiari I malformation are typically brief (< 5 min.), occipital, and associated with cough/Valsalva and lower brainstem or cerebellar symptoms (e.g., dysphagia, dysarthria, ataxia). This patient’s headaches are associated with vomiting and last hours, are typical during the day, and often resolve with sleep, all features that are typically associated with migraine, a much more prevalent type of headache. Brain imaging is warranted when there are symptoms that could be due to elevated intracranial pressure, such as nighttime headaches and vomiting, the MRI shows no evidence for hydrocephalus, and there is no papilledema on exam. Nor is there a history of positional headache to suggest intracranial hypotension (treated with caffeine in some cases). Thus, the most reasonable approach would be to treat the patient for presumed migraine headaches with a prophylactic agent and an alternative abortive therapy (ibuprofen), as acetaminophen is not providing adequate relief. Incorrect Options: Option A - Intravenous caffeine : This option is not the most reasonable next step in this case. Intravenous caffeine might be considered for the acute treatment of certain types of headaches, but in this scenario, the boy's symptoms and MRI findings suggest a different condition. The displaced cerebellar tonsils are indicative of a condition known as Chiari malformation, and the headaches and other symptoms are likely related to this condition. Option B - Lumbar puncture to evaluate for intracranial hypertension : While lumbar puncture can be used to evaluate for increased intracranial pressure, it might not be necessary in this case. The boy's symptoms and MRI findings are more consistent with a structural issue (Chiari malformation) rather than increased intracranial pressure. Option C - Referral to neurosurgery for posterior fossa decompression : This could be a potential management option for the boy's condition. questions.stem: A 35-year-old female presents with shortness of breath, wheezing, and chest tightness. She has a past medical history of asthma and is currently taking a short-acting beta-agonist (SABA) as needed. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.stemHtml: A 35-year-old female presents with shortness of breath, wheezing, and chest tightness. She has a past medical history of asthma and is currently taking a short-acting beta-agonist (SABA) as needed. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Start inhaled corticosteroids (ICS): Asthma management involves a combination of medication and lifestyle modifications to control symptoms and prevent exacerbations. The treatment approach is individualized based on the severity of the disease, frequency and severity of symptoms, and the patient's age and comorbidities. Inhaled corticosteroids (ICS): These are the most effective anti-inflammatory medications used in the treatment of asthma. They work by reducing airway inflammation and preventing exacerbations. ICS are usually prescribed as the first-line treatment for patients with persistent asthma. Short-acting beta-agonists (SABAs): These medications act as bronchodilators and are used to provide quick relief of symptoms such as cough, wheeze, and shortness of breath. They are usually prescribed as a rescue medication for patients with intermittent asthma or as a quick-relief medication for those with persistent asthma. Long-acting beta-agonists (LABAs): These medications are also bronchodilators but have a longer duration of action compared to SABAs. They are used in combination with ICS for patients with moderate to severe persistent asthma. Leukotriene modifiers: These medications block the action of leukotrienes, which are substances that contribute to airway inflammation. They are usually prescribed as an alternative to ICS for patients with mild persistent asthma or as an add-on therapy for those with moderate to severe persistent asthma. Theophylline: This medication relaxes the smooth muscles of the airways and improves airway function. It is usually prescribed as an add-on therapy for patients with moderate to severe persistent asthma. Incorrect Options: Option A - Prescribe a long-acting beta-agonist (LABA): Adding a LABA to SABA monotherapy is not recommended as first-line therapy for asthma control. LABAs are generally used in combination with ICS to provide additional control when ICS alone is insufficient.   • Inhaled corticosteroids (ICS): These are the most effective anti-inflammatory medications used in the treatment of asthma. They work by reducing airway inflammation and preventing exacerbations. ICS are usually prescribed as the first-line treatment for patients with persistent asthma.
  • Short-acting beta-agonists (SABAs): These medications act as bronchodilators and are used to provide quick relief of symptoms such as cough, wheeze, and shortness of breath. questions.solution: Correct Option B- ST-segment elevation in leads II III aVF: This patient’s bradycardia on initial presentation and a second-degree heart block later on suggests inferior wall myocardial infarction. Inferior wall MI will present as ST-segment elevation in leads II, III, and aVF. The branches of the right coronary artery supply the inferior wall of the heart. The posterior descending artery (PDA) supplies the AV node and arises from the RCA in 90% of the cases (right dominant circulation). Infraction of the inferior wall will result in systolic dysfunction of the right ventricle , resulting in decreased preload into the left ventricle and hence a fall in the cardiac output. Therefore a patient who develops a second-degree heart block after myocardial infarction has undergone an inferior wall infarction in the majority of cases. AV block due to MI will resolve in 8-10 days . In symptomatic patients following options are available: IV Atropine (0.6mg) Temporary pacemaker Incorrect Options: Option A- ST-segment elevation in leads I aVL: ST-segment elevation in leads I, aVL represents lateral wall MI. The left circumflex artery (LCX) supplies the heart's lateral wall. The posterior descending artery will arise from LCX in less than 10% of the cases (left dominant circulation). This patient’s angiography revealed a right dominant circulation, so he likely suffered from an inferior wall MI. Option C- Sawtooth appearance of waves: Atrial flutter is characterized by a large re-entry circuit near the cavotricuspid isthmus in the right atrium. The atrial rate is usually 300/min. ECG will show a characteristic sawtooth appearance of the flutter waves. Treatment options include: Catheter ablation Rate control by digoxin, β-blockers, or verapamil. Rhythm control using DC cardioversion. Anticoagulation according to the CHA2DS2-VASc scoring system. Option D- Diffuse ST-segment elevation with PR depression: Acute pericarditis results from the inflammation of the pericardium and is characterized by diffuse ST-segment elevation and/or PR depression. The typical presentation is a retrosternal chest pain that radiates to the neck and shoulders, aggravated by breathing and relieved by leaning forward . Fever is also common. Some of the important causes include the following: Viral infection Malignancy Systemic lupus erythematosus Uremia Myocardial infarction ECG findings include: Widespread ST elevation with upward concavity PR depression T wave inversion may be found after some time Treatment options include: NSAIDs Colchicine Glucocorticoids Pericardiocentesis in case of large effusions. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Which of the following markers would not be helpful in the diagnosis of a neuroendocrine carcinoma?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following markers would not be helpful in the diagnosis of a neuroendocrine carcinoma?
questions.solution: Correct Option D - PAX8: PAX8 is a transcription factor that plays a crucial role in the development of various organs, including the thyroid, kidney, and female reproductive system. Immunohistochemical staining for PAX8 is commonly used to identify tumors originating from these organs. PAX8 is not a marker for neuroendocrine differentiation. It is primarily used to identify tumors of müllerian origin (e.g., endometrial adenocarcinoma, ovarian serous carcinoma) and is not associated with neuroendocrine tumors. Therefore, in the context of diagnosing a neuroendocrine carcinoma, PAX8 staining would not provide relevant information. questions.stemHtml: A 62-year-old male patient with a smoking history and hyperlipidemia underwent coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) surgery for triple-vessel coronary artery disease. The patient is now postoperative day 4 and has developed a fever. Labs reveal an elevated white blood cell count. On examination, the patient's sternum is tender to palpation with a purulent discharge from the surgical incision site. What is the most likely complication of CABG in this patient?
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Deep sternal wound infection: Sternal wound infection is a potentially serious complication that can occur after coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) surgery . It is an infection of the incision site in the chest where the sternum is divided to access the heart. The infection can be superficial , involving only the skin and subcutaneous tissue, or deep , involving the bones and internal organs. The incidence of sternal wound infection after CABG is between 0.5% and 5%, and the risk factors include obesity, diabetes, smoking, immunosuppression, prolonged ventilation, and emergency surgery. The signs and symptoms of sternal wound infection include fever, pain, redness, swelling, tenderness, and drainage from the incision site. Treating sternal wound infection includes . The antibiotics used depend on the severity of the infection and the causative organisms, which may include Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus species, and Gram-negative bacteria . Wound care involves regular dressing changes, debridement of necrotic tissue, and vacuum-assisted closure therapy . In some cases, surgical intervention may be required to remove infected tissue and close the wound. Recognizing and promptly treating sternal wound infection is important to prevent serious complications such as mediastinitis, sepsis, and death. Incorrect Options: Option A - Bleeding: Bleeding is a possible complication of CABG, but the patient's symptoms and examination findings are more suggestive of a surgical site infection. Option B - Stroke: Stroke is a possible complication of CABG, but it typically occurs during the procedure or in the immediate postoperative period. Option C - Myocardial infarction: Myocardial infarction is a possible complication of CABG, but it typically occurs during or immediately after the procedure , not on postoperative day 4. The patient's symptoms and examination findings suggest a surgical site infection. @Neet_pg_bot

Tularemia is a zoonotic infectious disease caused by the bacterium Francisella tularensis. It is known for its ability to infect a wide range of animals, including rabbits, rodents, birds, and insects, and can be transmitted to humans through various routes, such as tick bites, handling infected animals, and inhaling contaminated aerosols. This bacterium appears as small, pleomorphic, gram-negative rods or coccobacilli in clinical samples and is often difficult to visualize on Gram stain due to its small size and tendency to stain poorly. questions.solution: Correct Option A - Hypercalcemia: In banked blood, citrate is used as an anticoagulant. If units of blood are transfused too fast or the patient has liver dysfunction, then there is a risk of overwhelming the body with citrate that can bind calcium, causing hypocalcemia. Incorrect Options: Option B - Metabolic alkalosis: Citrate in banked blood will be metabolized by the liver into bicarbonate, which may lead to a metabolic alkalosis. However, if blood is infused rapidly or there is liver dysfunction, then metabolism is overwhelmed and is not sufficient. In this case citrate itself can cause a metabolic acidosis. Option C - Hypokalemia: As red cells begin active metabolism, potassium is actively taken up by these cells and may result in hypokalemia. Option D - Hypothermia: If blood products are not warmed, it may lower the body temperature, causing hypothermia. Hypothermia may cause worsening coagulopathy as well. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option B: Cardiac Output (CO) Oxygen Saturation in Venous Blood (SvO2) Left Ventricular End Diastolic Volume (LVEDV) Pulmonary Capillary Wedge Pressure (PCWP) Low Low High High This patient’s symptoms point toward a diagnosis of systolic heart failure. His features like the history of myocardial infarction, smoking, shortness of breath, crackles, extra heart sound, oedema and ejection fraction of 30% are ample information to diagnose heart failure with reduced ejection fraction. It is logical to think that the cardiac output (CO) would be reduced when there is a reduction in ejection fraction. Oxygen saturation in venous blood is reduced in low-output states primarily because blood becomes stagnant in the peripheral vasculature due to the inability of the heart to pump properly and body tissues extract the oxygen out of the blood, thus leaving low oxygen saturation in the venous blood. Since the heart has a reduced ejection fraction, more blood will be left in its cavity after every contraction of the left ventricle. Consequently, at the end of diastole, there will be a large left ventricular end diastolic volume (LVEDV). Pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP) is a parameter measured by inserting a catheter in the pulmonary vasculature via the right-sided heart. It blocks a pulmonary vessel and measures the pressure at that level. For all practical purposes, this measurement is considered equivalent to the pressure in the left atrium. So, PCWP is basically a measure of left atrial pressure. If we imagine a backlog of blood due to the incapacity of the left ventricle to pump effectively, we can see the PCWP rising in this patient. Heart failure in which there is a reduced ejection fraction can be due to several causes, the most common being myocardial infarction followed by dilated cardiomyopathy and arrhythmias. Incorrect Options: Option A: Cardiac Output (CO) Oxygen Saturation in Venous Blood (SvO2) Left Ventricular End Diastolic Volume (LVEDV) Pulmonary Capillary Wedge Pressure (PCWP) Low High Low Low This combination can be seen in the late stages of septic shock when the heart cannot pump at a higher CO. Oxygen Saturation in Venous Blood (SvO2) is high due to the inability of the tissues to extract oxygen from the blood in the case of septic shock. LVEDV will be reduced due to pooling in the vasculature and PCWP will be low for the same reason. Option C: Cardiac Output (CO) Oxygen Saturation in Venous Blood (SvO2) Left Ventricular End Diastolic Volume (LVEDV) Pulmonary Capillary Wedge Pressure (PCWP) Low Low Low Low This combination is seen in hypovolemic shock. Due to lower blood volume, stroke volume is low, thus low CO. As less blood reaches the left atrium and ventricle, PCWP and LVEDV are also reduced. SvO2 is also reduced as the tissues extract oxygen out of the blood. Option D: Cardiac Output (CO) Oxygen Saturation in Venous Blood (SvO2) Left Ventricular End Diastolic Volume (LVEDV) Pulmonary Capillary Wedge Pressure (PCWP) Low Low Low Normal This combination is commonly seen in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction. SvO2 is reduced due to oxygen extraction by body tissues. As there is concentric hypertrophy, the LVEDV is reduced and PCWP is normal. Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction is secondary to hypertension not myocardial infarction. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml:
A three-year-old girl is referred to you for evaluation of several months of progressive gait issues. There is no abnormality on the skin examination over her lumbosacral spine, but imaging reveals a low-lying conus medullaris, consistent with tethered cord syndrome.

questions.solution: Correct Option B - Lipomyelomeningocele: Tethered cord syndrome can occur in the setting of both open and occult neural tube defects. Occult spinal dysraphisms have no open defect, but there may be abnormalities of the skin, such as discoloration or a tuft of hair, at the site of the underlying defect. Occult dysraphisms include lipoma, lipomyelomeningocele, dermal sinus, and diastematomyelia (split cord). Open neural tube defects include meningocele (spinal fluid and arachnoid herniate through a dural defect), myelomeningocele (spinal cord tissue, spinal fluid, and arachnoid herniate through defect), hemimyelomeningocele, and myeloschisis (exposed neural tissue without overlying membrane). Incorrect Options: Option A - Hemimyelomeningocele: This is an open neural tube defect where only one half of the spinal cord and its associated structures protrudes through the defect in the vertebral column. It is not associated with occult spinal dysraphism. Option C - Meningocele: This is an open neural tube defect where the spinal fluid and meninges (protective coverings of the spinal cord) herniate through a dural defect. It is not typically associated with tethered cord syndrome. Option D - Myelomeningocele: This is the most severe form of open neural tube defect, where the spinal cord tissue, spinal fluid, and meninges herniate through a defect in the vertebral column. While tethered cord syndrome can develop in individuals with myelomeningocele, the question is specifically asking about an occult spinal dysraphism associated with tethered cord. Myelomeningocele is not an occult condition. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option D - Lurbinectedin: The current recommendation for patients relapsed within 6 months of treatment is Lurbinectedin. Lurbinectedin is an alkylating agent that is FDA approved for patients with metastatic small cell lung cancer (SCLC) with disease progression on or after platinum-based chemotherapy. This approval is based on a single-arm, open-label, phase 2 basket trial of patients with SCLC (no brain metastases) who progressed on or after platinum-based chemotherapy. With a median follow-up of 17.1 months they reported the following: Overall response rate (ORR) with lurbinectedin: 35.2% Median duration of response: was 5.3 months Patients still responding at 6 months: 43.0% Overall response rate (ORR) among patients with chemotherapy-free interval <90 days: 22% vs. 45% among patients with a chemotherapy-free interval ≥90 days 12 month overall survival among patients with chemotherapy-free interval <90 days: 12.9% vs. 48.3% among patients with a chemotherapy-free interval ≥90 days All patients in this study received a prespecified antiemetic regimen consisting of a corticosteroid and serotonin antagonist. Serious adverse reactions occurred in 10 percent of patients, of which neutropenia and febrile neutropenia were the most common (5 percent for each). Incorrect Options: Option A - Paclitaxel: Paclitaxel is a chemotherapy drug commonly used in the treatment of various cancers, including lung cancer. While it has shown activity against some solid tumour’s, including lung cancer, it is not commonly used as a standard treatment for extensive-stage SCLC. questions.stem: A 62-year-old female presents to your clinic for additional evaluation. She was recently diagnosed with FIGO Stage IA1 squamous cell of the cervix. She recently had a cone biopsy, and the results of the pathology show that there is no sign of lymph vascular space invasion (LVSI) and that the biopsy margins are free of invasive illness. Given this information which of the following would be the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.stemHtml: A 62-year-old female presents to your clinic for additional evaluation. She was recently diagnosed with FIGO Stage IA1 squamous cell of the cervix. She recently had a cone biopsy, and the results of the pathology show that there is no sign of lymph vascular space invasion (LVSI) and that the biopsy margins are free of invasive illness. Given this information which of the following would be the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: C
options.text: Modified radical hysterectomy with pelvic lymph node dissection

options.label: D
options.text: Modified radical hysterectomy without pelvic lymph node dissection

questions.solution: Correct Option B - Extra fascial hysterectomy: The below recommendations are based on current NCCN guidelines: Stage IA1 cervical cancer represents a disease confined to the uterus that is microscopic with a depth of stromal invasion of ≤ 3 mm and horizontal spread of ≤ 7 mm. Options for operable patients with stage IA1 disease depend on the results of the cone biopsy and preferences for fertility preservation. For patients with IA1 disease with no lymphovascular space invasion (LVSI) and negative invasive disease margins (or positive dysplasia at the margin) after cone biopsy, extra fascial hysterectomy can be performed. For those with positive invasive margins or LVSI, a modified radical hysterectomy with pelvic lymph node dissection should be performed. For IA1 patients who desire fertility preservation, cone biopsy alone can be performed if margins are negative (> 3 mm preferred) and no LVSI is present. For IA1 patients desiring fertility preservation with LVSI, radical trachelectomy (removal of cervix and parametria with cerclage placed, leaves the uterus intact) with lymph node dissection can be performed. Patients with dysplasia have many treatment options including conization, loop electrosurgical excisional procedure (LEEP), laser ablation, cryotherapy, or extra fascial hysterectomy. For positive margins, modified radical hysterectomy is also an option. Incorrect Options: Option A - Observation: Observation might be considered in certain cases of very early-stage cervical cancer, but given that the patient has already been diagnosed with FIGO Stage IA1 squamous cell carcinoma, active intervention is typically recommended. Option C - Modified Radical Hysterectomy with Pelvic Lymph Node Dissection: Modified radical hysterectomy with pelvic lymph node dissection might be considered for higher-stage or more aggressive forms of cervical cancer, but for a FIGO Stage IA1 squamous cell carcinoma with no evidence of LVSI and negative margins, this level of surgical intervention is typically not necessary. Option D - Modified Radical Hysterectomy without Pelvic Lymph Node Dissection: Given the favorable characteristics of the tumor (FIGO Stage IA1, no LVSI, and negative margins), a modified radical hysterectomy without pelvic lymph node dissection is usually sufficient for this stage of the disease. Lymph node dissection might be considered if there were higher-risk features, but it's not typically recommended for this scenario. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option B - Lack of cortisol: This patient's presentation is most consistent with primary adrenal insufficiency complicated by adrenal crisis during endoscopy. His history of weight loss, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea and anorexia shows primary adrenal insufficiency. During endoscopy, he suddenly had hypotension and shock due to acute adrenal insufficiency, also called adrenal crisis. The most common causes of the adrenal crisis are adrenal hemorrhage, adrenal infection, injury, and surgery in patients with chronic adrenal insufficiency. The treatment involves hydrocortisone or dexamethasone (preferred) and is accompanied by rapid intravenous volume repletion. His jugular vein pressure (also known as JVP) was found to be high throughout the assessment. The JVP rises to a higher level upon inspiration. Which of the following is most likely to explain this finding?
questions.stemHtml: A 62-year-old man who has a previous medical history of heart failure comes into the emergency department complaining of chest pain and breathlessness. His jugular vein pressure (also known as JVP) was found to be high throughout the assessment. The JVP rises to a higher level upon inspiration. Which of the following is most likely to explain this finding?
questions.solution: Correct Option D- Constrictive pericarditis: In a patient who suffers from heart failure, breathlessness, and chest discomfort, constrictive pericarditis is the most likely condition, which is associated with increased jugular venous pressure (JVP) that rises upon inspiration. This finding is known as Kussmaul's sign and is considered pathognomonic for constrictive pericarditis. Constrictive pericarditis is characterized by the thickening and stiffening of the pericardium, the sac-like membrane surrounding the heart. This causes constriction of the heart, leading to impaired diastolic filling and subsequent right-sided heart failure. One of the most common signs of constrictive pericarditis is elevated JVP. There is an increase in venous return during inspiration that contributes to the subsequent rise in JVP that occurs during inspiration. Incorrect Options: Option A- Cardiac tamponade: Cardiac tamponade is characterized by the accumulation of fluid in the pericardial sac, which can cause heart compression and decrease cardiac output. This can result in symptoms such as shortness of breath, chest pain, and hemodynamic instability. In cardiac tamponade, elevated jugular venous pressure (JVP) is common due to impaired filling and increased central venous pressure. However, unlike in constrictive pericarditis, the JVP typically decreases upon inspiration due to the reduced venous return during inspiration. This finding is known as pulsus paradoxus and a hallmark of cardiac tamponade. Option B- Acute myocardial infarction: Acute myocardial infarction is a life-threatening emergency that happens when a coronary artery suddenly gets blocked, leading to myocardial ischemia and necrosis. The classic symptoms are pain or discomfort in the chest radiating to the jaw or left arm, shortness of breath, sweating, diaphoresis, and nausea or vomiting. Acute myocardial infarction can lead to heart failure, which can cause elevated JVP, but the associated inspiratory increase is not a feature of AMI. Therefore, in the case presented, acute myocardial infarction (B) is not likely to be associated with an elevated JVP that increases upon inspiration. Option C- Pulmonary embolism: PE can cause right-sided heart failure, leading to elevated jugular venous pressure (JVP). However, an elevated JVP that increases upon inspiration is not typically seen in PE. JVP may be normal or even decreased in PE, especially in cases of massive PE. @Neet_pg_bot

Esophageal pressure topography reveals a type I OGJ, integrated relaxation pressure (IRP) of 10 mmHg, and distal latency of 5.8 seconds. His study indicates distal contractile integral (DCI) of 9000 mm/s/cm on 2 swallows with single-peaked contraction. This is characteristic of which of the following?
questions.stemHtml: A patient with dysphagia undergoes high-resolution manometry. Esophageal pressure topography reveals a type I OGJ, integrated relaxation pressure (IRP) of 10 mmHg, and distal latency of 5.8 seconds. His study indicates distal contractile integral (DCI) of 9000 mm/s/cm on 2 swallows with single-peaked contraction. This is characteristic of which of the following?
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Jackhammer esophagus: Jackhammer or hypercontractile esophagus is characterized by 2/10 test swallows with a DCI >8000 mm/s/cm. The Chicago Classification scheme of esophageal motility diagnosis categorizes motility disorders based on esophageal pressure topography studies. EGJ morphology is not a defining criteria for motility studies but can identify a hiatus hernia. A hiatus hernia can distort EPT metrics. Basal EGJ pressure is also not a defining criterion but in some disorders it can be pertinent, including GERD and achalasia. Type I EGJ is normal. IRP is based on the median value of 10 test swallows and is a major diagnostic criterion for achalasia and EGJ outflow obstruction. Integrated relaxation pressure measures adequacy of LES relaxation with swallowing. Abnormal IRP is consistent with esophageal motility disorders and is defined as the average minimum EGJ pressure for 4 seconds within seconds of swallowing. In patients with hypercontractile esophagus, the IRP is normal. The upper limit of normal is 15 mmHg. Incorrect Options: Option A - Normal esophageal motility: The DCI is elevated in >20% of test swallows, indicating hypercontractile jackhammer esophagus. Option B - GERD: GERD is not a motility disorder of the esophagus. Option D - Type I achalasia: Patients with type I achalasia have an IRP at or above the upper limit of normal, and no contractility is present. @Neet_pg_bot

Hemoglobin has dropped from a baseline of 9.8 g/dL to 6.2 g/dL. Patient is given 3 units of packed red blood cells. Which of the following would be the least appropriate therapy ?
questions.stemHtml: A 17-year-old female with a diagnosis of type III von Willebrand disease is admitted to the hospital with a lower G.I. bleed. Hemoglobin has dropped from a baseline of 9.8 g/dL to 6.2 g/dL. Patient is given 3 units of packed red blood cells. Which of the following would be the least appropriate therapy ?
questions.solution: Correct Option - DDAVP (Desmopressin): DDAVP (Desmopressin) is not an appropriate therapy for patients with type III von Willebrand disease. Type III von Willebrand disease is characterized by a complete deficiency of von Willebrand factor (vWF). Unlike patients with type I or type II von Willebrand disease, patients with type III lack the necessary storage pool of vWF in endothelial cells or megakaryocytes. DDAVP works by releasing stored vWF from endothelial cells, which can then aid in hemostasis. Since patients with type III von Willebrand disease have no stored vWF, DDAVP is not effective in increasing vWF levels in these individuals. Therefore, the expected finding on renal biopsy would be subepithelial deposits with basement membrane thickening. Membranous nephropathy is characterised by the thickening of the glomerular basement membrane, which leads to proteinuria and impaired kidney function. It is one of the most common causes of nephrotic syndrome in adults. It may be caused by antibodies to phospholipase A2 receptors (present in the glomerular basement membrane) or associated with other underlying conditions, such as infections, autoimmune diseases (SLE), and cancer. Incorrect Options: Option B- Segmental sclerosis and hyalinosis of glomeruli: This finding is consistent with focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) , another type of glomerulonephritis. FSGS is characterised by damage to the podocytes , specialised cells in the glomerulus that help filter the blood. This can result in segmental sclerosis (scarring) and hyalinosis (deposition of a pink, amorphous material) within the glomeruli. On renal biopsy, this would appear as focal areas of scarring and hyalinosis within the glomeruli. However, phospholipase A2 receptor antibodies are associated with membranous nephropathy, characterised by glomerular basement membrane thickening with subepithelial deposits. Option C- Subendothelial deposits with a tram-track appearance: This finding is consistent with membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN). This type of glomerulonephritis is characterised by the proliferation of mesangial cells and the deposition of immune complexes in the glomerulus. On renal biopsy, this would appear as s ubendothelial deposits with a "tram-track" appearance due to the splitting of the basement membrane between the deposits. Underlying conditions, such as subacute and chronic infection, including hepatitis B and C, syphilis, subacute bacterial endocarditis, autoimmune diseases, and genetic disorders , can cause it. Option D- Crescent-shaped deposits in the glomeruli: This finding is consistent with rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (RPGN), a type of glomerulonephritis characterised by a rapid decline in kidney function over days to weeks. RPGN is usually associated with a crescentic appearance of the glomeruli on renal biopsy. These crescents are composed of fibrin and inflammatory cells , such as macrophages and glomerular parietal cells and are seen in Goodpasture syndrome, Wegener granulomatosis, and microscopic polyangiitis . It is not associated with antibodies to phospholipase A2 receptors. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option A - Von-Hippel-Lindau syndrome: This patient’s clinical features and imaging findings suggest Von Hippel Lindau syndrome. Increased levels of metanephrine in the urine and suprarenal mass suggest pheochromocytoma. Von hippel-lindau syndrome is an inherited condition that involves multiple systems and organs. A mutation in the von hippel-lindau tumour suppressor gene causes it. This gene is located on chromosome number three. Signs and symptoms include headaches, balance and walking problems, weakness of limbs, vision problems, elevated blood pressure, and dizziness. It is associated with many tumours and cysts like a pancreatic and renal cysts, cerebellar hemangioblastoma, renal cell carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, and neuroendocrine tumour of the pancreas. Pheochromocytoma is also associated with other genetic disorders like multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (MEN 2), Von hippel-lindau disease (VLH), neurofibromatosis 1 (NF1), and hereditary paraganglioma syndrome. Incorrect Options: Option B - Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1: Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN1) is associated with primary hyperparathyroidism and pituitary and pancreatic tumours. Signs and symptoms of MEN1 include fatigue, joint and muscular pain, gastric ulcers, and renal stones. This patient’s signs and symptoms indicate VPL. Option C - Lynch syndrome: Lynch syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder . It is a genetic condition that significantly increases the risk of many cancers, such as colon and endometrial. Mutations in mismatch repair genes cause it. Lynch syndrome is characterised by a colon or endometrial cancer development before the age of 50. These patients also have a positive family history of cancer before age 50. This patient’s cerebellar hemangioblastoma, bilateral renal cysts, and pheochromocytoma suggest the diagnosis of VPL. Option D - Krukenberg tumour: It is a gastric carcinoma which is composed of signet ring cells. This tumour usually spreads through the lymphatic channels into the ovaries, known as the krukenberg tumour. Signs and symptoms of the krukenberg tumour include abdominal mass, pain in the abdomen, weight loss, menstrual irregularities, vaginal bleeding, and pain with sexual intercourse. She also reports seeing halos around lights when looking out of her right eye. questions.solution: Correct Option A - Angle-closure glaucoma: Angle-closure glaucoma (ACG) is a rare idiosyncratic reaction to certain medications including topiramate. Despite being uncommon, it can lead to permanent visual loss if untreated so it’s important that physicians be aware of this possible complication. Presenting symptoms include severe eye pain, headache, nausea, vomiting, and seeing halos around lights. Examination may reveal conjunctival redness, a poorly reactive mid-dilated pupil, a shallow anterior chamber and corneal edema. Emergency treatment by an ophthalmologist is key to preserving vision, and involves immediate cessation of the offending medication, use of topical medications to lower intraocular pressure and laser peripheral iridotomy. Incorrect Options: Option B - Cluster headache: Cluster headache can cause pain around the eye associated with unilateral autonomic symptoms. In this case, the temporal proximity to starting topiramate, and the associated visual symptoms make angle-closure glaucoma a more likely diagnosis. Option C - Migraine headache: Migraine headache is in the differential diagnosis of any unilateral headache syndrome but the clinical presentation including conjunctival injection and pupillary changes argue against migraine. Option D - Dry eye: Dry eye can lead to eye pain, but severe acute eye pain with nausea and vomiting, associated with pupillary changes would not be consistent with this diagnosis. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option B - Growth of the mandible and soft tissues of the face: The patient with the presenting complaints of hyperhidrosis, skin tags, and increased shoe and finger size has most likely the diagnosis with acromegaly. Acromegaly or gigantism occur due to the hypersecretion of the growth hormone. When growth hormone hypersecretion occurs before the fusion of long bone, then gigantism occurs. When the hormone hypersecretion occurs after the fusion of epiphysis, causing large extremities and characteristic faces, it causes acromegaly. The hallmark feature of acromegaly is the overgrowth of bones and soft tissues, particularly in the face and extremities. This leads to a number of characteristic physical features, including an enlarged jaw (prognathism), thickening of the skin, and enlargement of the hands and feet. However, long bone growth is not affected in acromegaly because the growth plates have already fused in adults. Option C - Growth of the hands and feet: Growth of the hands and feet is partially correct because acromegaly does lead to enlargement of the hands and feet due to overgrowth of soft tissues, but not the bones themselves. Option D - Growth of the thorax and abdomen: Growth of the thorax and abdomen is also partially correct because acromegaly can cause enlargement of the organs in the thorax and abdomen, such as the heart and liver, but not the bones themselves. @Neet_pg_bot

In contrast, non-classic, a milder form, usually presents in childhood or adolescence. questions.solution: Correct Option C - Pneumocystis jiroveci: The patient presents with the clinical features and investigative findings of Pneumocystis pneumonia. It usually occurs in immunocompromised patients (HIV/AIDS and leukemic patients). The main presenting feature of Pneumocystis pneumonia is progressive dyspnoea. Dry cough and fever are also common . The chest x-ray is normal initially and shows bilateral interstitial infiltrate spreading out from the hilar regions later. HRCT ( high-resolution CT scan) is more sensitive and shows ‘ground-glass’ interstitial infiltrates. Pneumatocele, if present, may rupture, leading to pneumothorax . Diagnosis is based on silver stains, polymerase chain reaction (PCR), or immunofluorescence of broncho-alveolar lavage or induced sputum. Treatment is with high-dose co-trimoxazole with or without corticosteroids. Incorrect Options: Option A - Streptococcus pneumoniae: Streptococcus pneumoniae is the most common cause of community-acquired pneumonia. It is not associated with pneumonia in an immunocompromised individual, and bilateral interstitial infiltrates on chest x-ray. Option B - Mycoplasma pneumoniae: Mycoplasma pneumoniae causes community-acquired pneumonia in young, healthy individuals. It presents with non-specific changes on chest x-ray, such as localized reticulonodular opacities, parahilar or peribronchial infiltrates, lobar consolidation, and mixed interstitial and focal airspace pneumonia at multiple sites . It is less likely to cause pneumonia in an immunocompromised patient. questions.solution: Correct Option A - Nuclear oligomerization domain (NOD): NOD is a cytosolic receptor for pathogen associated molecular patterns (PAMP). PAMPs are bacterial and viral components recognized by mucosal antigen presenting cells. Their detection leads to cytokine secretion and initiation of an inflammatory reaction to control the infection. Option C - Major histocompatibility complex (MHC): MHC is a surface receptor on antigen presenting cells. Option D - CX3CR1: CX3CR1 is a surface chemokine receptor. Polymeric Ig receptor (also called secretory) is expressed on the surface of intestinal epithelial cells and binds dimeric IgA or IgM. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option A - Corticosteroids: Physiologically, corticosteroids decrease the inflammatory response by inhibition of inflammatory cells and release of proinflammatory mediators and cytokines. In the emergency department, corticosteroids are indicated for all moderate to severe attacks or those that don’t respond completely to initial short-acting beta agonists such as the patient in this scenario. Corticosteroid onset of action is within hours of administration during an attack and peaks at approximately 24 hours. Asthmatics have a multifold positive response, such as increased resolution of exacerbation, reduced relapses, and possibly decreased admission rates for those with severe attacks. Incorrect Options: Option B - Magnesium sulfate: Use of magnesium sulfate should be limited to patients with severe asthma who require ICU care. Option C - Montelukast: Montelukast is a leukotriene receptor antagonist that is less effective than inhaled glucocorticoids in most patients. Data does not support routine use of montelukast therapy in children with acute asthma exacerbations who require urgent or emergent care. Option D - Terbutaline: Terbutaline is an intravenous beta agonist that can potentially be useful in combination with an inhaled beta agonist in severely ill patients who are poorly responsive to conventional therapy. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option D - All of the above Daratumumab, a monoclonal antibody used in the treatment of multiple myeloma, has a multifaceted mechanism of action that involves various immune-related processes, including: Incorrect Options: Option A - Antibody-Dependent Cell-Mediated Cytotoxicity (ADCC) : Daratumumab can bind to CD38, which is highly expressed on the surface of multiple myeloma cells. When daratumumab binds to CD38 on myeloma cells, it facilitates the recognition of these cells by immune effector cells, such as natural killer (NK) cells. NK cells then engage and destroy the myeloma cells, leading to cytotoxicity. Option B - Antibody-Dependent Cellular Phagocytosis (ADCP) : In addition to ADCC, daratumumab can also stimulate antibody-dependent cellular phagocytosis. This mechanism involves the binding of daratumumab to CD38 on myeloma cells, which makes the myeloma cells more susceptible to being engulfed and destroyed by phagocytic immune cells, such as macrophages. Option C - Complement-Dependent Cytotoxicity and Apoptosis : Daratumumab can activate the complement system, which is part of the innate immune response. Activation of the complement system can lead to the lysis (breakdown) of myeloma cells, contributing to their destruction. Additionally, daratumumab can induce apoptosis (programmed cell death) in myeloma cells, further promoting their elimination. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 53-year-old woman with history of HIV, T2DM, and CKD disease on peritoneal dialysis presented with abdominal distention and mild fever. USG ( abd) revealed normal size and contour of the liver, normal gallbladder, and moderate sized ascites. Abdominal paracentesis was performed, which showed low serum to ascites albumin gradient (<1.1 g/dL) and high protein concentration. WBC count in ascites fluid was 500 cells/μL, with a lymphocytic predominance. Cytology did not reveal any malignant cells. Furthermore, serum CA-125 as well as ascites-fluid adenosine deaminase levels were elevated. What is the most likely diagnosis?

USG ( abd) revealed normal size and contour of the liver, normal gallbladder, and moderate sized ascites. Abdominal paracentesis was performed, which showed low serum to ascites albumin gradient (&lt;1.1 g/dL) and high protein concentration. WBC count in ascites fluid was 500 cells/μL, with a lymphocytic predominance. Cytology did not reveal any malignant cells. Furthermore, serum CA-125 as well as ascites-fluid adenosine deaminase levels were elevated. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: Correct Option A- Tuberculosis peritonitis: Risk factors for tuberculosis peritonitis include cirrhosis, HIV, underlying malignancy, and diabetes mellitus. Patients have elevated ascites WBC counts with lymphocytic predominance, along with high adenosine deaminase levels. This can differentiate between peritoneal carcinomatosis and tuberculosis peritonitis. Cytology will be positive in more than 90% of the cases of peritoneal carcinomatosis. Cirrhotic patients are at risk for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis. This condition is usually associated with high serum to ascites albumin gradient and high WBC counts in ascites fluid analysis. Secondary bacterial peritonitis usually is polymicrobial and is associated with high neutrophil counts in ascites fluid. Fungal peritonitis usually is associated with high WBC count and neutrophilic predominance in ascites fluid. Incorrect Options: Option B- Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP): Is unlikely in this case since the WBC count in the ascites fluid is not highly elevated, and there is a lymphocytic predominance rather than the typical neutrophilic predominance seen in SBP. Option C- Metastatic ovarian cancer: Is less likely because the patient's history, laboratory findings, and adenosine deaminase levels in ascites fluid are more suggestive of an inflammatory process, such as tuberculosis. Option D- Fungal peritonitis: Is less likely as there are no specific indications of fungal infection in the provided information. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 70 year-old-male from a remote village is referred to your OPD with a recent diagnosis of small cell lung cancer. You tell him that the current standard of care would be twice a day radiation therapy with concurrent cisplatin and etoposide (4-6 cycles given every 3 weeks). As he comes from a remote village, he asks you what effect once-daily radiation therapy would have on his outcome. Which of the following would be the most accurate median survival comparing once vs. twice daily radiation therapy with concurrent cisplatin and etoposide?
questions.stemHtml: A 70 year-old-male from a remote village is referred to your OPD with a recent diagnosis of small cell lung cancer. You tell him that the current standard of care would be twice a day radiation therapy with concurrent cisplatin and etoposide (4-6 cycles given every 3 weeks). As he comes from a remote village, he asks you what effect once-daily radiation therapy would have on his outcome. Which of the following would be the most accurate median survival comparing once vs. twice daily radiation therapy with concurrent cisplatin and etoposide?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - 30 months twice-daily vs. 25 months once-daily (p=non-significant): The most accurate response to this question can be found based on the results of the CONVERT trial. In this trial, patients with limited-stage small cell lung cancer were randomized to twice a day radiation therapy 45 Gy (1.5 Gy twice daily x 30 fractions) vs. once daily radiation therapy 66 Gy (2 Gy once daily x 33 fractions) starting with cycle 2 of cisplatin/etoposide chemotherapy (given 4-6 cycles q3weeks). Median overall survival was 30 months for twice-daily vs. 25 months for once-daily (p=0.14).Most toxicities were similar between the groups, except higher grade 4 neutropenia with twice-daily RT. Incorrect Options: Option B - 45 months twice-daily vs. 40 months once-daily (p=non-significant): This option presents similar information to the first option, but with longer median survival times for both groups. However, the key concept here is that the survival difference is not statistically significant. Option C - 30 months twice-daily vs. 15 months once-daily (p=significant): This option suggests a significant difference in survival between the two groups, with a lower median survival of 15 months for those receiving once-daily radiation therapy. However, this contradicts the idea that once-daily radiation therapy is considered a standard of care and is associated with worse outcomes. Option D - 60 months twice-daily vs. 25 months once-daily (p=significant): This option implies a significant difference in survival with a notably higher median survival of 60 months for those receiving twice-daily radiation therapy. Again, this contradicts the established understanding of the standard of care for small cell lung cancer. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option B - Secondary Hyperparathyroidism: The above-mentioned case is secondary hyperparathyroidism , as the patient is a case of end-stage renal disease , having a history of hemodialysis . Laboratory investigations reveal hypocalcemia and hyperphosphatemia. ECG changes also favour the diagnosis. The most important cause of secondary hyperparathyroidism is chronic kidney disease; others include malabsorption syndromes , osteomalacia and rickets . The patient presents with complaints of myalgias , abdominal pain , having a history of renal disease , and may also complain of multiple fractures . Laboratory investigations include hypocalcemia , hyperphosphatemia , and reduced 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol levels . Reduced calcium levels are a stimulus for the parathyroid gland, the parathyroid gland becomes enlarged, leading to tertiary hyperparathyroidism. Treatment strategies include symptomatic management, vitamin D supplements , a low phosphate diet , phosphate binders and eventually surgical intervention in case of treatment failure. Incorrect Options: Option A - Primary Hyperparathyroidism: Primary hyperparathyroidism is characterised by raised parathyroid and calcium levels, and has multiple causes; the most common is an adenoma, while others are nodular sclerosis and carcinoma. Radiological investigations show degenerative joint changes and osteoclastic or lytic lesions in the skeleton. Treatment includes surgical excision of the adenoma. Option C - Tertiary Hyperparathyroidism: Tertiary hyperparathyroidism is characterised by raised calcium levels and variable parathyroid hormone levels. The secondary may lead to autonomous parathyroid hormone production occurring and converted to tertiary hyperparathyroidism. Cinacalcet is the drug of choice. Option D - Hypoparathyroidism: Hypoparathyroidism occurs as a result of a post-surgery complication of thyroid surgery and is also associated with multiple autoimmune diseases. questions.solution: Correct Option C - Hyperplasia of pulmonary vascular walls Hypertrophy and hyperplasia of pulmonary vascular walls is the underlying cause of pulmonary artery hypertension. It is caused by the toxicity of the sympathomimetic effect of cocaine abuse. The most common presentation of pulmonary artery hypertension is dyspnea on exertion. On examination, the pulmonic component of S2 (Second heart sound) is loud. The complication of pulmonary artery hypertension is right ventricular hypertrophy which ultimately leads to the cor pulmonale (Right ventricular failure). Incorrect Options: Option A - Calcification of the pulmonary valve Pulmonary valve calcification can cause pulmonary stenosis. It leads to the splitting of S2. Option B - Hypertrophy of interventricular septum Hypertrophy of the interventricular septum is seen in hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy. In hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy the S2 is loud but not the pulmonic component. Furthermore, S4 would also be expected. This patient also has no family history of sudden cardiac death. Option D - Obstructive sleep apnea This patient’s BMI is normal and obstructive sleep apnea is unlikely in patients with normal BMI.
